title: Least squares, maximum likelihood and weighted least squares on the same model
promptMarkdown:
Consider $y_i = \theta x_i + \epsilon_i$, $i = 1, \dots, N$, as in W1D2 Tutorials 1–2.

1. Derive the least-squares estimator $\hat\theta_{LS}$ by minimising $\sum_i (y_i - \theta x_i)^2$. Check that your stationary point is a minimum.
2. Assume $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ independently with $\sigma$ unknown. Write the log-likelihood $\ell(\theta, \sigma^2)$ and show that the MLE of $\theta$ equals $\hat\theta_{LS}$. Derive the MLE of $\sigma^2$ and say whether it is unbiased.
3. Now assume $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_i^2)$ with known, unequal $\sigma_i$. Derive the MLE of $\theta$ and explain in one sentence what it does that $\hat\theta_{LS}$ does not.
4. Synthetic data (constructed for this exercise, not measured): $(x, y) = (1, 1.1), (2, 2.3), (3, 3.1)$. Compute $\hat\theta_{LS}$ as an exact fraction and as a decimal, the residuals, and $\hat\sigma^2_{MLE}$. Then recompute $\hat\theta$ with $\sigma_i = 0.1, 0.2, 0.3$ and comment on which point moved the estimate and why.
hintLadder: Differentiate the sum of squares with respect to $\theta$ and set it to zero; the second derivative is $2\sum x_i^2 > 0$.
The Gaussian log-density of $y_i$ is $-\tfrac12\ln(2\pi\sigma^2) - (y_i - \theta x_i)^2/(2\sigma^2)$; sum over $i$ and note which terms depend on $\theta$.
With unequal variances each squared residual is divided by its own $\sigma_i^2$; the weights $1/\sigma_i^2$ carry through the derivative.
For the small dataset, $\sum x_iy_i = 1.1 + 4.6 + 9.3$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 14$.

deterministicChecks.description: weights 1/σ_i² appear in the heteroscedastic estimator
the estimators must be derived for general N, not read off the three points

criteria.criterion: θ̂_LS = Σx_iy_i/Σx_i² from the first-order condition, with the second derivative 2Σx_i² > 0 confirming a minimum.
ℓ = −(N/2)ln(2πσ²) − Σ(y_i − θx_i)²/(2σ²); ∂ℓ/∂θ = 0 gives θ̂_LS; σ̂²_MLE = SSR/N, biased (E = σ²(N − 1)/N here since one parameter is fitted).

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: θ equivalence shown, σ² or bias wrong.

criteria.criterion: θ̂_W = Σ(x_iy_i/σ_i²)/Σ(x_i²/σ_i²): precise points weigh more; ordinary least squares treats all points as equally reliable.
θ̂ = 15/14 = 1.0714; residuals 0.029, 0.157, −0.114; σ̂² = 0.0386/3 = 0.0129; weighted θ̂ = 1.094, pulled towards the first point (slope 1.1), which has the smallest σ.

checkExamples.label: correct derivation
checkExamples.text: For general N, d/dθ Σ(y_i − θx_i)² = −2Σx_i(y_i − θx_i) = 0 gives θ̂_LS = Σx_iy_i/Σx_i², a minimum since the second derivative 2Σx_i² > 0. Log-likelihood ℓ = −(N/2)ln(2πσ²) − Σ(y_i − θx_i)²/(2σ²); the only θ-dependence is through the sum of squares, so the MLE of θ is θ̂_LS; ∂ℓ/∂σ² = 0 gives σ̂² = SSR/N, which is biased (expected value σ²(N−1)/N). With known σ_i, ℓ = const − Σ(y_i − θx_i)²/(2σ_i²), so θ̂_W = Σ(x_iy_i/σ_i²)/Σ(x_i²/σ_i²): precise points count more, which plain least squares ignores. Numbers: Σxy = 15.0, Σx² = 14, θ̂ = 15/14 = 1.0714; residuals 0.029, 0.157, −0.114; SSR = 0.0386, σ̂² = 0.0129. Weighted: θ̂ = 1.094, pulled towards the first point, whose slope y/x = 1.1 and whose σ = 0.1 gives it weight 100.

checkExamples.label: slope by eye and no weighting
checkExamples.text: Looking at the points the slope is about 1.5. The variances do not matter because least squares is always the best estimator.
